gap: No result ChatGPT got says that, of its four picks, only the Epoch 24V 100Ah publishes a surge figure (200 A for 60 seconds) or a continuous rating above 100 A (120 A, about 3,072 W at 25.6 V). The headline cycle counts of the four picks also can't be compared: none states the capacity left at end of life, and only LiTime states a depth of discharge (100%).
standout_why: I opened the cited Solar Powered Project comparison and the top-ranked Gesike US 24V roundup. Solar Powered Project covers only 12V batteries, so it has no Epoch, LiTime or Redodo 24V figures. It warns that cycle claims at different depths of discharge can't be compared, but it doesn't convert them to a common basis. Gesike lists every 24V model at 100 A / 2,560 W continuous and says surge is 'not stated' for every model except GSIKE. It doesn't cover Epoch at all and never mentions end-of-life capacity. Ryzzun's LiTime 24V review says LiTime lists no peak current. ChatGPT's own answer says a 3,000 W inverter may need a higher discharge rating, but it doesn't say which pick has one. Score kept at 2, not 3: I couldn't read the other rival pages (SolarKitHQ, BatteryTrail, GearRanking, Charge-Test), and I couldn't confirm Redodo's or LiTime's surge spec on their own maker pages.
decides: This mostly confirms the picks and adds one real limit. At the 25.6 V nominal voltage, a 100 A BMS (LiTime, Redodo) caps a single battery at about 2,560 W. That's below a 3,000 W inverter even before inverter losses. Epoch's 120 A continuous gives about 3,072 W. That still falls short once you allow about 10% inverter loss (a 3,000 W load then draws about 130 A), but Epoch's 200 A for 60 seconds covers motor starts and compressor kicks. Epoch is the premium pick for high-draw or cold-weather installs, and a single LiTime or Redodo fits loads up to about 2,000 W unless you add a second battery in parallel. On cycle life, Epoch's 3,500+ looks lower than LiTime's 4,000+ at 100% depth of discharge. Neither states end-of-life capacity, and Epoch's page puts its test conditions in a datasheet I couldn't read, so the headline numbers shouldn't decide between them.

findings.label: Continuous discharge
findings.note: Maker's US page. Watts = 120 A × 25.6 V nominal. A 3,000 W AC load at about 90% inverter efficiency draws about 3,333 W ÷ 25.6 V ≈ 130 A, which is above 120 A.

findings.label: Surge discharge
findings.note: Maker's US page. The 60-second window is much longer than the 1–5 s peak ratings other brands use (the cited Solar Powered Project page lists 12V peaks of 300 A for 5 s, 400 A for 1 s and 200 A for 2 s), so peak amps alone aren't comparable across brands. Invertersrus.com shows the same 200 A (60 s).
